slides.0.title: Regulatory change and Diploma essays
slides.0.subtitle: From Coteaux du Languedoc to the pyramid, and essay structures
slides.1.title: Regulatory timeline
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Before 2007
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Coteaux du Languedoc was recognised by decree of 24 December 1985; whites were allowed across the appellation in 1988; 2004 saw geographic denominations such as Terrasses du Larzac
slides.1.highlights.1.title: 2007 and 2023
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Renamed Languedoc on 30 April 2007, adding zones such as Corbières; the current specification was approved on 30 November 2023 (Languedoc AOC page)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Independent AOCs
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Terrasses du Larzac 2014, La Clape 2015 and Pic Saint-Loup 2017; in 2024 La Livinière and Boutenac were registered in the EU Official Journal as AOPs
slides.1.content: Each promotion is a step from regional wine toward village wine.
slides.2.title: The pyramid and DGCs
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The current pyramid
slides.2.highlights.0.content: AOP Languedoc and DGCs at the base, sub-regional AOPs in the middle and communal AOPs on top (Languedoc AOC page); whether the CIVL 2010 three-tier model still applies is not stated
slides.2.highlights.1.title: 11 DGCs, five communal
slides.2.highlights.1.content: DGCs include Cabrières, Grès de Montpellier, La Méjanelle, Montpeyroux, Pézenas, Quatourze, Saint-Christol, Saint-Drézéry, Saint-Georges-d'Orques, Saint-Saturnin and Sommières; communal AOPs include Boutenac, Faugères, La Clape, La Livinière and Montpeyroux
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Montpeyroux still changing
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The Languedoc AOC page says INAO confirmed standalone status in February 2026, with the decree and European Commission sign-off still pending as of March 2026; it lists Montpeyroux as both DGC and communal, so it is not tested
slides.2.content: A status in transition should be written as in transition, not as settled.
slides.3.title: How rules tighten
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Raising minimums
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Maury's Grenache Noir minimum rose from 50% at creation to 75% now (Wikipedia; the year of change is not stated)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: New categories
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Maury Sec has allowed dry table wine from the same varieties since the 2011 vintage; Saint-Chinian introduced a white in 2004; Picpoul de Pinet has its own specification from 23 September 2013
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Renamings and mergers
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Languedoc-Roussillon merged into Occitanie in 2016; Rivesaltes combined several smaller designations in 1972 (Wikipedia)
slides.3.content: Tighter rules come with finer names, a common path in Languedoc.
slides.4.title: Essay structures
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Type 1: quality transformation
slides.4.highlights.0.content: "Evaluate Languedoc's shift from bulk to quality": context (wine lake, vine-pull) → tools (new AOCs, DGCs, IGP) → results and limits (area decline, crisis) → conclusion
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Type 2: climate adaptation
slides.4.highlights.1.content: "Discuss the threats and opportunities of climate change for Languedoc-Roussillon": threats (drought, heat, fire) → opportunities (cooler uplands, organic, resistant varieties) → rule flexibility (AOC varieties and irrigation) → conclusion
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Type 3: system design
slides.4.highlights.2.content: "Is the coexistence of AOC and IGP an asset or a burden?": AOC clarity, IGP flexibility (58 varieties), consumer confusion, export performance
slides.4.content: Back every argument with one concrete example that has a year or number.
slides.5.title: Short-answer practice: question and marking points
slides.5.highlights.0.title: Question 1
slides.5.highlights.0.content: “Explain how the grape-proportion rules of Languedoc AOCs shape wine style, using Pic Saint-Loup and Fitou as examples.” (about 250 words)
slides.5.highlights.1.title: Marking points for question 1
slides.5.highlights.1.content: ① Languedoc AOC reds: main varieties at least 50%, Mourvèdre plus Syrah at least 20%, Carignan and Cinsaut each capped at 40%; ② Pic Saint-Loup: Syrah at least 50%, cool and wet (about 900–1,000 mm) → fresher, spicier; ③ Fitou: Carignan at least 40%, average about 40 hL/ha → old vines, concentration, rustic power; ④ winemaking: Carignan often made by carbonic maceration to soften tannins; ⑤ conclusion: proportion rules, yields and style are locked together
slides.5.highlights.2.title: Question 2
slides.5.highlights.2.content: “Is the coexistence of AOC and IGP an advantage or a burden for the Languedoc? Assess.” (about 350 words)
slides.5.highlights.3.title: Marking points for question 2
slides.5.highlights.3.content: ① IGP Pays d’Oc: about 120,000 ha, 58 varieties, 85% varietal labelling → the engine of exports and varietal wine; ② AOC: new AOCs and DGCs (Terrasses du Larzac 2014, La Clape 2015, Pic Saint-Loup 2017) build village-level recognition; ③ burden: too many names and consumer confusion, and in crises (grubbing-up schemes, falling exports) price pressure passes through the co-operatives; ④ conclusion: complementary roles, but high communication costs
slides.5.content: The keyword for assessment questions is “division of labour”: say who serves whom, then discuss the costs.
